subject: Dedicated footprint & ramp alternatives — Helio Health capacity plan
messages:
From: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.ai>
To: Pete Alvarez <pete@heliohealth.ai>
Cc: Emma Liu <emma@heliohealth.ai>
Date: Wed, 1 Nov 2028 10:03:00 -0700
Subject: Dedicated footprint & ramp alternatives — Helio Health capacity plan

Hi Pete / Emma —

Thanks again for the time this morning. Attached is a compact proposal with three reserved-capacity options calibrated to the workload you shared (inference mix: 60% chat, 30% batch-embedding, 10% reranking). Summary up front so you can digest quickly: 

- Option A (Conservative): 8 reserved GPUs minimum, staggered 3-month ramp to 24 GPUs. Lowest upfront commit; recommended if you want low burn and flexibility.
- Option B (Balanced): 16 reserved GPUs minimum, predictable throughput for steady production; 6-month ramp to 48 GPUs with burst lanes.
- Option C (Aggressive): 32 reserved GPUs minimum, aggressive performance SLO (99th %ile latency target), phased to 96 GPUs over 9 months; best unit-cost at scale.

Key implementation notes:
- We recommend prefix caching + steady-state batching for chat to keep latency inside SLO while reducing token cost.
- For model variants we suggest pinning the 2 most compatible quantized builds for automatic fallback.
- Warm lanes: include 10% hot standby capacity to absorb peak bursts without cold starts.

I've included the raw GPU sizing workbook and a one-page ramp chart in the attachments. Can you confirm which option you'd like us to model into a mutual action plan? If you want, we can prepare a small 30-day pilot on Option A to validate traffic/latency assumptions before committing.

Thanks —
Jordan Blake
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference

From: Pete Alvarez <pete@heliohealth.ai>

Subject: Re: Dedicated footprint & ramp alternatives — Helio Health capacity plan

Jordan —

Appreciate the clear options. Quick questions before we loop procurement: 

1) For Option B, what is the expected steady-state token cost per 1M chat tokens vs Option A? Rough percent difference is fine.
2) For Option C, we expect some model changes in Q2 — how brittle is the aggressive commit if we switch model family (e.g., 70B -> 100B)? Any re-quantization/compatibility risk and how would that affect our SLA?
3) Can you provide an explicit warm-start credit or burn-rate protection if we have a slow adoption period after signature? Procurement will ask.

If possible, send a one-page summary table we can forward internally. Looking to get procurement involved by next week.

—Pete
Pete Alvarez
Head of ML Platforms, Helio Health

Karthik / Soojin —

Forwarding Pete's questions from Helio. Can you confirm the following and I'll send Pete a concise table:

- Percent token-cost delta: Option A -> B, and B -> C (ballpark).
- Compatibility guidance if customer moves from a 70B class model to 100B mid-contract (quantization/variant risks and recommended fallback policies).

Thanks —
Jordan
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.ai>, Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.ai>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 2 Nov 2028 14:22:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Fwd: Dedicated footprint & ramp alternatives — Helio Health capacity plan

Jordan / Soojin —

Notes from engineering/solutions POV below. I'll keep it short so we can paste into a 1-pager: 

- Cost delta (ballpark):
  • Option A -> B: ~18–25% lower per-token cost at steady state (mainly due to better GPU utilization and more aggressive batching).
  • Option B -> C: additional ~12–18% reduction (scale efficiencies + reserved pricing on our side).

- Model-family switches (70B -> 100B):
  • Risk: moving to a larger model increases memory/KV cache pressure. A naive 100B build may require different kernel selection and could reduce effective batch sizes, increasing per-token latency/cost.
  • Mitigation: we recommend maintaining a paired quantized variant (e.g., 4-bit optimized) and a fallback smaller-family variant for high tail loads. Our runtime can automatically route to the fallback under high memory pressure. Expect a short re-qualification window (2–4 weeks) to validate quantized kernels and performance profiles.

- Warm-start credit suggestion:
  • Offer a 60-day ramp credit equal to 30% of committed monthly spend for months 1–2 (applies only if actual usage is below 50% of the committed baseline).
  • Credit redemption can be used against future invoices during the first 6 months. This protects Helio during slow adoption while maintaining incentive to scale.

- Operational recommendation: include a canary traffic policy for the first 30 days after each activation milestone (validate latency and throughput at each 25% ramp step).

Happy to make this tighter for procurement; I can draft the one-pager if you want.

—Karthik
Principal Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Dedicated footprint & ramp alternatives — Helio Health capacity plan

Pete / Emma —

Thanks for the questions. Per Karthik's notes above, attached is a one-page comparison table and the proposed warm-start credit language we can include in the SOW. Quick summary and next steps: 

- Recommended commercial path: Option B (Balanced) + 60-day 30% warm-start credit. This gives Helio predictable performance while preserving a path to scale to Option C within 6–9 months.
- Pilot alternative: 30-day pilot on Option A (8 GPUs steady, telemetry access) if you want a low-risk validation first.
- Action items:
  1) If procurement is comfortable with the warm-start credit, we can issue redlines and a DocuSign-ready SOW by Monday. (Related link: https://docsend.com/d/helio-reserved-proposal-v1-2)
  2) Karthik / Soojin to run a quick model re-qualification plan if you decide to onboard 100B-class models.

I'll queue the DocuSign package as soon as I get a thumbs up.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Head of Sales Operations, Redwood Inference
